podcast.body: Elvis's live performance in 1955 profoundly influenced Buddy Holly, convincing him to dedicate his career to becoming a rock and roll star. Holly's promoter, a friend of Elvis's, added Buddy and Bob to the bill, leading to frequent hangouts between Holly and Elvis. podcast.title: Appearance and Impact (1950s)
podcast.body: Elvis came along in the 1950s, captivating millions of post-war kids, who were then emerging as "teenagers." His music, a blend of blues, country, and R&B, was played on new radio stations and greatly annoyed their parents, which made it dangerous, forbidden, and therefore very attractive to the youth. "Elvis came along in the 1950s, just as millions of post-war kids, these new constructs that were now being called teenagers, began gravitating to new radio stations that played music derived from a mix of the blues, country and R&B."

xref.title: First Recording at Sun Studios (1953)
xref.body: On July 18, 1953, a young truck driver named Elvis Presley recorded two songs, "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" and "My Happiness," at Sun Studios in Memphis as a birthday present for his mother. These were Elvis Presley's first recordings ever, and based on this session, studio head Sam Phillips helped Elvis become the iconic figure he would be. This record is argued to be the genesis of all rock and roll. Jack White later purchased this one-of-a-kind artifact for $305,000 US, subsequently digitizing and re-releasing it through Third Man Records so the world could hear it. "This is on July 18th, 1953, a young truck driver dropped into Sun Studios in Memphis to record himself singing a song for his mother."

xref.title: My Aim Is True (1977) – Debut Album Recorded by Clover, Who Became Huey Lewis and the News
xref.body: Before his music career, Elvis Costello worked as a computer operator for Elizabeth Arden cosmetics, running invoices on an IBM 360 mainframe, taking occasional sick days to demo songs. When he signed to Stiff Records, he needed a backing band. An American group called Clover had just arrived in England hoping for their big break, but found themselves stranded in the middle of punk and unwanted. They needed money for plane tickets home. Elvis went to their residency at Headley Grange, told them he needed a studio band and specifically didn't need a singer, so Clover's own singer was sent to wait elsewhere while the rest of the band backed Elvis through six four-hour sessions for his debut. Clover was paid and sent back to the US, where they reinvented themselves as Huey Lewis and the News. The singer who had to hang out during the Costello sessions was Huey Lewis. "That banished singer was Huey Lewis."

xref.title: Saturday Night Live Act of Defiance (December 17, 1977)
xref.body: Elvis Costello's North American breakthrough came when he was a last-minute replacement musical guest on Saturday Night Live on December 17, 1977, after the Sex Pistols faced visa issues. NBC insisted he play his British hit "Less Than Zero" and avoid "Radio, Radio," which was critical of radio (a sensitive topic given NBC's radio station ownership). Costello feigned agreement but defiantly launched into "Radio, Radio" live on air, an "act of corporate nose thumming" that inspired thousands. "That act of defiance, that act of corporate nose thumming inspired thousands."

xref.title: Disastrous American Tour – January 1978
xref.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren's plan to "conquer America" with the Sex Pistols resulted in one of rock history's most disastrous road trips. Initially, the group's visa applications were denied, forcing them to cancel an important appearance on Saturday Night Live, where Elvis Costello was called in as a last-minute replacement. The drummer for Elvis Costello's performance notably wore a t-shirt that read "Thanks, milk," a sarcastic jab at Malcolm McLaren. McLaren made a bizarre miscalculation about American culture by routing the tour away from major cities and through the deep South, an area not receptive to punk rock values. "Instead, what he got was one of the most disastrous road trips in the history of rock."

xref.title: Columbus Holiday Inn Bar Fight (March 10, 1979) – Racist Remarks, Punch from Bonnie Bramlett, Career Nearly Ruined in America
xref.body: On March 10, 1979, Elvis Costello and his entourage were drinking heavily in a bar at a Holiday Inn in Columbus, Ohio, when they encountered Stephen Stills's party. Costello made blatant racist remarks about Ray Charles and James Brown. Stephen Stills's companion Bonnie Bramlett punched Costello, a full brawl broke out, and the incident made national news. American media sided with Stills; Costello became toxic and his American career took years to recover. He later described the incident in his memoirs *Unfaithful Music and Disappearing Ink* (2015) and acknowledged it without denial or excuse. "An old barfight from 37 years ago — but there are real serious things that haven't been fixed that are not my doing or my responsibility."

xref.title: Refusal to Play Encores

"Elvis Presley refused to do Encore's. Hence the famous Elvis has left the building announcement, designed to clear out fans who wanted more."

xref.title: Robert Smith's Early Influences
xref.body: Robert Smith's older siblings introduced him to a diverse range of artists, including The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, Captain Beefheart, David Bowie, Jimi Hendrix, and Nick Drake. The subsequent arrival of punk rock, with bands like Sex Pistols, Ramones, and Elvis Costello, further shaped his musical direction and helped him find his artistic niche. "His older brother and sister had filled his head with beetles and stone songs, but they also subjected him to a lot of Captain B-Fart, and David Bowie, and Jimmy Hendrix and Nick Drake. And then when punk came along, it was Sex Pistols Ramones Elvis Costello. Young Robert found his niche."

xref.title: Robert Smith's Influences
xref.body: Robert Smith's musical upbringing was shaped by his older brother and sister, who introduced him to The Beatles and The Rolling Stones. xref.body: Little Richard is argued to be rock's first openly gay rock star, or at least bisexual with strong gay leanings. xref.title: Stiff Records Signing and Name Change
xref.body: After a period as a folk singer and a member of Flip City, Declan McManus (then calling himself DP Costello) sent out numerous demo tapes and received many rejections before becoming the very first artist signed to the newly formed Stiff Records. It was Stiff Records' boss, Jake River Yara, who famously dubbed him "Elvis Costello." xref.title: Uncredited Backing Band for Elvis Costello
xref.body: Clover was an American band that found itself broke while touring the UK. They were hired by Jake Riviera of Stiff Records to back Elvis Costello on his debut album, My Aim Is True, recording through late 1976 and early 1977 in a tiny studio in Islington, London. Due to contractual issues (another British band was already named Clover), they used the pseudonym The Sham Rocks and were never credited on the original album release.
